cells.tense: The ending is here, and you're standing in it without a fight.
cells.ask: Close one finished thing today, all the way, and leave the space open until something asks for it — offering yourself the ease of a grip actually released.
cells.core: On an ordinary day, the finished thing gets put down and left down: the account closed, the box handed on, the thanks said once, and then you eat your dinner. You finish it, you let it be finished, and you don't carry it around while something new is starting. That's what release looks like when it's working — no wake held, no story kept, no hand still on the door. It isn't that nothing's hard here. Setting down something that used to matter still costs you. But you're not bargaining with the ending or leaning on it, and this ease is free to feed whatever comes next.
cells.sheetLine: You let the finished thing be finished, and you don't carry it forward.
cells.place: the ending that has to be real before anything else starts

cells.tense: You're already living in the ending that hasn't come, rehearsing the surrender before you've had to make it.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're still in the middle of and finish it today instead of walking away from it — then see what finishing, rather than leaving early, gives you back.
cells.core: On a day this is working, you can put something down cleanly and stay long enough to know it's done. One finished thing, no theatre, the ending small and real. What's happening instead is that you're bracing ahead of time: you set things down before you've had to, and the setting down is becoming its own performance. Saying no to things you could still carry. Withdrawing before anyone can ask. There's a reason that can feel like protection — if you're the one walking out first, the ending can't be taken from you. But the cost is that nothing gets to run its course, including the things worth keeping. Finishing is what this is for, and it hasn't been reached.
cells.sheetLine: You're letting go early, because walking out first feels safer than letting something end on its own terms.
cells.place: the ending that has to be real before anything else starts

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door that closed behind you, and your grip hasn't moved off the handle.
cells.ask: Keep one thing you're still carrying this week on purpose — not to carry it forever, just to feel what sustaining it actually takes — and see what knowing the real weight gives you back.
cells.core: On a day this is working, the thing ends and your hands open. The old role, the old plan, the old version of someone gets set down, and you can look at what's coming without the old weight in your arms. What's happening instead is that your grip is still closed — not from stubbornness but because setting something down has come to feel like dropping something that will break, so you keep on and the keeping is tiring you out. Someone else's bad mood, someone else's failure, a decision you keep not making: you've taken it as your job to keep it from landing. Keeping one thing steady on purpose, and knowing you're the one keeping it, is how this gets built back. That's not the same as being crushed by it.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding something that already ended, and the keeping has become your whole job.
cells.place: the ending that has to be real before anything else starts

cells.tense: The ending has already happened, and you're still talking about it as if it hasn't.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, that one thing you've already let go of — name the ending as yours — and see what saying it plainly gives back to you.
cells.core: On an ordinary day you can feel the difference between something that's over and something that's still going, and you act on it. You already act on it in some places: there's a thing you've stopped turning over, a hope you've stopped staking your next year on, and you can feel it's gone quiet. What hasn't happened is calling it what it is. You keep describing the ending as 'still figuring it out', or the release as something other people did, when it was you who stopped. Naming it doesn't make it more final — it just puts the say-so back where it belongs. It's already running. The only question is whether you'll admit it's yours.
cells.sheetLine: You've already let go of something you keep describing as still in the air.
cells.place: the ending that has to be real before anything else starts
